The large wall behind the Centennial Plaza is located adjacent to the Port Union Community Recreation Centre, lending colour and history to a busy community hub. The project was produced by Mural Routes, in partnership with the Centennial Community and Recreation Association and StreetARToronto.
ImageAltText: A section of a large mural depicting a historic scene on a creek of a First Nations settlement with people around a fire and in canoes, and a man hunting.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: In 1946, to meet the large demand for housing with the postwar baby boom, a few of the GECo buildings, mainly on Civic Road (south of Eglinton between Warden Avenue and Birchmount Road), were converted into temporary housing for returned soldiers and their families. A few years later, many of those people were transferred into the newly built Regent Park housing development in downtown Toronto.
ImageAltText: A black and white historical photograph depicting an aerial view of many munitions buildings on an industrial site at Warden Avenue and Civic Road.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: This mural was painted on Youthlinks' exterior in 2012 by Mural Routes as part of the Leadership Training in Mural Making program. Elaine Teguibon developed the concept of the mural, which uses puzzle pieces to represent the links and connectivity of people, communities and organizations. It was painted by artists Rob Matejka, Elaine Teguibon, Tara Dorey and Raymond Cho with support from youth employment program artists.
ImageAltText: On the front and side exterior walls of the Youthlinks building, a mural with panels shaped like puzzle pieces depicting youth engaged in various activities.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Painted by Canadian street artist Omen, this StreetARToronto and Mural Routes collaboration pays homage to Scarborough's history. The north wall, Bomb Girls, honours women who worked in a nearby munitions plant during the Second World War. Built and run by the General Engineering Company (GECo), the plant was located south of Eglinton Avenue between Birchmount Road and Warden Avenue. The south wall, Scarboro Junction, pays tribute to Scarborough Junction's historical sites, including the Everest & Sons General Store and Scarborough Junction Station built in 1873.
Address: St. Clair Ave. E. underpass, east of Warden Ave.
ImageAltText: An underpass retaining wall is covered by a painted mural that features black and white portraits of women from the nineteen fourties against a colourful background.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Metamorphosis is based on the themes of change and transformation. Situated at the entrance, it brings positivity to the Warden Woods Community Centre. Lead artist Tara Dorey and Mural Routes' artists led local youth in a series of stencil-making workshops to create the images of the stages of a butterfly's life and transformation. In addition, there are silhouetted natural scenes in the walkway's inner walls. Visiting artist Redzuan Salleh, from Singapore, designed and painted the outer wall with the help of local youth.
ImageAltText: On the side of an exterior entrance ramp to the Warden Woods Community Centre, a painted mural depicting people silhouetted against an outdoor landscape, and two hands releasing a dove.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Flight explores themes of migration, transition and change inspired by the migration of the monarch butterfly. This mural was created from several wood panels, which were put together like a puzzle. It was created as part of the Mural Routes Summer Youth Mural Program and painted by artists Thea Chow, Rob Matejka, Fathima Mohiudden, Katy Mulla and Minal Patel.
ImageAltText: An exterior brick wall with a panelled mural that depicts the Toronto skyline, an assortment of monarch butterfies, cocoons and caterpillars, and human figures.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Created by Mural Routes in partnership with the City of Toronto, this underpass mural was painted by artist De Anne Lamirande to celebrate Scarborough history. The west wall shows the iconic Bluffs and Elizabeth Simcoe, the woman who gave Scarborough its name, while the east wall depicts the historic Bell Estate. The Bell Estate is a cut fieldstone house built in 1830 for the Thornbeck family. It was sold to the Bell family in 1882, who went on to establish Bell's Scarboro Dairy on the property, which served much of the local neighbourhood. Birch trees fill the south centre column and oak trees fill the north centre column, a symbolic joining of the Birch Cliff neighbourhood and Oakridge community.
Address: Warden Ave. railway underpass, south of Danforth Ave.
ImageAltText: A painted mural on the walls and pillars of an underpass features a portrait of Elizabeth Simcoe, two trees and a steam train at a station with passengers.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: This mural was created as a part of Birch Cliff Community Mural Project. Mural Routes artist Rob Matejka designed the mural and artists Tara Dorey and Anthony Delacruz, with youth artists, painted this larger-than-life birch tree in a realistic style.
ImageAltText: On an exterior brick wall of an apartment building, a panelled mural of a birch tree trunk and forest spans three storeys.

SiteName: Bell Box Mural by Ruth Hurdle (2016)
Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: The birch tree motif in this mural by Ruth Hurdle incorporates beautiful fall foliage into its design. Look closely on the tree trunks to find letters, which spell out the street name Lynn.
ImageAltText: A Bell utility box covered by a painted mural of a birch forest with colourful autumn leaves on a rocky landscape overlooking a lake and mountains.

SiteName: The White Stag by Ted Hamer (2016)
Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: In painting this utility box as a part of the Bell Box Murals Project, artist Ted Hamer was inspired by stories of the white stag, a mythical being that will lead to profound consequences for those who see it. The white stag with golden antlers sits in a birch forest with autumnal colours.
ImageAltText: A Bell utility box covered by a painted mural of a white stag resting on green grass, surrounded by birch tree trunks and red vegetation in the background.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Artist Tara Dorey painted this mural as a part of Birch Cliff Community Mural Project continuing the birch tree motif. Here you'll see birch trees backed by forest and framed by soft blue sky.
ImageAltText: On the exterior side wall of a flower shop, a painted mural depicts a forest of birch trees against a pale blue sky.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Artist John Hood painted this mural as a tribute to the Scarborough Rifle Company, a 19th century militia. In 1862, the company was headquartered in a school building on Eglinton Avenue near Markham Road. It was the first of several militia companies formed in York County and saw active service on the Niagara frontier three times from 1865 to 1866, defending Canada against the Fenians, an Irish Republican organization that targeted British army forts in Canada to pressure Britain to withdraw from Ireland. The Scarborough Rifle Company later became the No. 1 Company of the 12th Battalion of Infantry, the forerunner of the Queen's York Rangers. The mural was restored in 2010 by Alan Bender.
ImageAltText: A mural covering the exterior wall of a building depicts a military procession with nineteenth century-era soldiers playing instruments, including brass and drums.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: This mural of birch trees bathed by the setting sun was painted and designed by artist Tara Dorey, and assisted by Emily Harrison and five youth employed at Mural Routes for the summer, as a part of Birch Cliff Community Mural Project.
ImageAltText: Close up of a panelled mural depicting birch trees, the Scarborough Bluffs and Lake Ontario shore, with the colours of a sunset in the sky.

SiteName: Bell Box Mural by Emily Harrison (2013)
Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Birch trees backed by a rural landscape and farmhouses brings this Bell utility box, painted by Emily Harrison, to life.
ImageAltText: Two utility pipes covered by a painted birch bark design, and behind them a Bell box covered by a mural depicting a forest of birch trees on a hillside with a creek.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Designed by artist Rob Matejka and painted by Mural Routes' youth artists, with support from StreetARToronto and Birch Cliff Public School Parent Council, the mural features three-storey-tall birch trees covering the east wall of the school.
ImageAltText: Behind a black metal fence, an exterior wall of Birch Cliff Public School is covered by a painted mural of ten birch trees that span three storeys.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: The two-storey mural on the storefront features birch trees and the nearby Scarborough Bluffs. Painted by Tara Dorey, this mural was created by Mural Routes with support from StreetARToronto.
ImageAltText: Close up of a painted mural on a storefront entranceway depicts birch trees with golden leaves and a lake and bluffs behind them.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Located here is another mural in the Birch Cliff Community Mural Project celebrating the beautiful birch trees and the Scarborough Bluffs. This one was created by Mural Routes and designed by Anthony Delacruz.
ImageAltText: The first storey exterior wall of a two-storey building is covered by a painted mural of the trunks of a dense birch forest against a colourful nature backdrop.

SiteName: Scarborough Arts, The Bluffs Gallery, Mural Routes and Monarch Butterfly Mural
Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: As a non-profit, local arts service organization, Scarborough Arts brings individuals and groups together to create and cultivate innovative arts and cultural programs in Scarborough. Step inside to see artwork by local and emerging artists in the Bluffs Gallery, run by Scarborough Arts. Scarborough Arts led a Signature Project for the 2018 Cultural Hotspot which celebrated central and north Scarborough and involved touring a large-scale Scarborough Sign, modelled after the Toronto Sign located at City Hall, to various sites around Scarborough to promote community pride.  Also located at this site, Mural Routes is responsible for the majority of the murals in Scarborough, including many of those featured on this tour. Mural Routes is the only member-based, not-for-profit arts service organization in Canada dedicated to the creation, development and promotion of public wall art. Two monarch butterfly murals adorn the Scarborough Arts building; one on the front door and the other on the garage door at the rear of the building, facing the parking lot. These murals were painted in 2003 by Mural Routes youth artists as a training exercise in preparation for creating the Flight mural at 395A Danforth Road. Enjoy the butterfly garden, created by artist B.C. Johnson, planted around the building.
ImageAltText: A black line illustration of a hip-roofed cottage with a central dormer window and a large chimney extending from the left side.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Sustenance is one of two gateway murals created as a Signature Project of the 2014 Cultural Hotspot. This beautiful mural, created by Bill Wrigley, focuses on the community's relationship with the bluffs overlooking Lake Ontario and the natural flora and fauna that thrive in the region. There is a focus on the migration of birds and butterflies. The Cathedral Bluffs are depicted on the left and the Scarborough Bluffs on the right. It was created in partnership with Mural Routes, StARToronto and the Cultural Hotspot.
Address: Kingston Rd. underpass at Danforth Ave.
ImageAltText: A colourful painted mural on the retaining wall of an underpass depicts the Scarborough Bluffs and shoreline with butterflies flying from one side to the other.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: The Scarborough War Memorial, constructed of limestone and bronze, is one of the oldest monuments in the south Scarborough area. It was erected in 1931 to honour soldiers fallen during the First World War. It was unveiled by Fleet Admiral Earl Jellicoe and Ontario Premier George S. Henry. Subsequent memorial plaques were added to honour those who fought in the Second World War and the Korean War.
ImageAltText: On a traffic island between two roads, the Scarborough War Memorial, a large limestone cross with an inset bronze sword, is mounted on a stone base with two visible inset plaques.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Painted by Jeff Jackson in 1992, this mural celebrates the Onondaga, a ship that was built near Kingston in 1790, and served as flagship of the Provincial Marine until her retirement seven years later. This was the ship in which Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe and his wife Elizabeth sailed across Lake Ontario, from Niagara-on-the-Lake to the town of York (now Toronto), to establish the capital of Upper Canada (now Ontario).
ImageAltText: The exterior wall of a two-storey building is covered by a pastel-coloured illustrated mural that depicts a large schooner ship sailing near the Scarborough Bluffs.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: These two murals, painted by Phillip Woolf, depict Spooner's Garage, an automobile garage, at two different times in its history: in 1926 and 1947. The owner of the garage, Art Spooner, sustained the business during the Great Depression in the 1930s by supplementing the business with driving lessons, a 24-hour towing service and even a restaurant.
ImageAltText: Painted mural covering the exterior side wall of a building, depicting the exterior of a 1920s garage and gas station with a blue car and its driver in front.

SiteName: The Bluffs As Viewed By Elizabeth Simcoe c. 1793
Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Painted by artist Risto Turunen, the mural depicts the Scarborough Bluffs rising from Lake Ontario, with a small boat below which represents the boat from which Elizabeth Simcoe, wife of Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe, first saw the bluffs. She was so impressed after seeing the bluffs that she convinced her husband to name the area after a town in England with similar looking cliffs. She wrote in her diary on August 4, 1793, "...after rowing a mile we came within sight of what is named in the map the highlands of Toronto. The shore is extremely bold and has the appearance of chalk cliffs... we talked of building a summer residence there and calling it Scarborough."
ImageAltText: A short, wide exterior wall of a building facing a parking lot features a painted mural of the Scarborough Bluffs and shoreline with people paddling a rowboat in the water.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: This area used to be the site of a golf course. The Cliffside Golf Club was started in 1931 by George McCordick, when he converted an old farmhouse into a clubhouse. It was closed in 1950 as new housing and commercial development spread along Kingston Road. The golf club had a beautiful view of Lake Ontario. The mural was painted by Dan Sawatzky and restored in 2011 as part of Mural Routes' leadership training program.
ImageAltText: A painted mural extending across the exterior side wall of a building depicts a nineteen-thirties golf course and club house with a car parked out front and a caddy and golfer about to play.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Working with themes of metamorphosis, transition and migration, members of a Scarborough storyteller group, Bluffers Tales, told a series of stories that celebrate the experiences of community members who immigrated to Canada. The artists incorporated these stories into the mural. The monarch butterfly is a central figure in the mural; a physical representation of metamorphosis. Chrysalis was created by Mural Routes, painted by artists Leah Burns, Katy Mulla and Ellen Bleiwas.
ImageAltText: The upper portion of an exterior wall is covered with a colourful painted mural featuring an oman's portrait, the Scarborough Bluffs, and a monarch butterfly, and inset to the right is a close up of another portion of the mural showing the words of a story and additional monarchs flying around it.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Created by John Hood, Half Way House depicts an inn of the same name that stood at the corner of Kingston Road and what is now Midland Avenue. Half Way House was a rural stage coach stop halfway between the village of Dunbarton and the St. Lawrence Market in Toronto. The building served many purposes before being moved to Black Creek Pioneer Village in 1965.
ImageAltText: The side wall of a two-storey brick building features a large painted mural depicting a historic streetscape with a stage coach and two-horse buggy in front of an inn with a veranda.

SiteName: Greeting to Taniperla (at the Scarboro Mission)
Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Greeting to Taniperla, initiated by the Red Tree Collective, is a re-creation of a mural painted in Chiapas, Mexico in 1998 by a group of Mayan villagers and later destroyed by Mexican armed forces. The imagery of the original Taniperla mural reflected on Tzeltal Mayan traditions and portrayed ideals of community life. In an act of solidarity, the mural of Taniperla has also been re-created in the towns of Rosario and Bariloche in Argentina. The Toronto project draws attention to the struggle in Chiapas and to issues affecting our own Indigenous communities. Painted by artists Lynn Hutchinson, Claire Carew, Raffael Iglesias, Shelley Niro, Hannah Claus, Sady Ducros with Scarborough youth.
ImageAltText: The outer walls of an outdoor handball court's cement enclosure are covered by a painted mural featuring informational text and images depicting ancient Mayans and Mayan cultural symbols.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: This commemorative mural, painted by Phil, Jennifer and Jamie Richards, depicts passengers boarding a radial car at Stop 17 on the Toronto and York Radial Line, which was located at the nearby junction of St. Clair Avenue and Kingston Road. In the background is Scarborough High School, now R.H. King Academy, which was built in 1922. The mural blends symbols of Scarborough's rural heritage with its development, with both a horse-drawn wagon and cow depicted alongside a radial car and gas-powered truck. This mural was a Scarborough Bicentennial project, initiated by the Cliffcrest Community Association and managed by Mural Routes.
ImageAltText: A painted mural on the wall of a brick building depicts a historical scene of a woman boarding a train with a horsedrawn wagon in the background.

Neighbourhood: Birchcliff, Birchmount Park, Cliffside, Scarborough Village
Description: Artist Lauren Kuzyk designed this mural to be inclusive, so that painters of all levels and experience were able to contribute. This beautiful rainbow-coloured mural represents the Scarborough Bluffs. This mural was created as a SPARK Project of Cultural Hotspot as part of Arts on the Road: The Kingston Road Creative Walk 2014. Arts Management students from R.H. King Academy worked together under the direction of Lauren Kuzyk.
ImageAltText: A painted mural on an exterior wall of a single-storey building depicts the Scarborough Bluffs in rainbow colours, a red location marker and the words "arts on the road".

Description: The Victoria Park Subway Station opened in 1968. It was one of only two subway stations to be found in Scarborough at the time. Victoria Park was also the second elevated subway station on the network (after Keele, which opened in 1966). The station was renovated in 2009 and reopened in 2010 and now features artwork by designer and environmentalist Aniko Meszaros as part of her installation entitled Roots. The mural depicts a multi-storey tree and root system on the platform stairwell, which was sandblasted into the existing ceramic tile. The word 'community' is written in different languages in circular globes.
ImageAltText: A painted mural on a tiled wall above a staircase features a tree made up of roots in various shades of green and printed in red overtop are the words "Diverse roots can grow and intermingle into a complex".

Description: The township of Scarborough acquired Warden Woods from the Sisters of St. Joseph in 1959. This thickly forested park escaped the clear-cut logging of much of the surrounding area and follows Taylor Massey Creek. It is home to a mature forest and wildlife, and features the Gus Harris Trail, which is named after Scarborough's fifth mayor. Follow the path to see the park's sand banks, which have been left exposed since a glacier formed the valley 12,000 years ago.
ImageAltText: In Warden Woods, a footbridge over a shallow stoney creek connects to a paved path and is surrounded by trees with colourful autumn leaves.

Description: Painted in early 1976 on the wall of MacMillan Auto Sales, the owl mural was a familiar neighbourhood landmark. The owner of MacMillan painted the original owl to go along with the then tagline of the business: 'make the wise choice.' Over time, the condition of the mural deteriorated. Artist De Anne Lamirande collaborated with the new building owner, Gary Bintsis, and painted Wise Owl to keep the neighbourhood icon. Lamirande incorporated the original tree and owl into a new colour scheme.
ImageAltText: Close up of a painted mural featuring a great horned owl sitting in a birch tree against a dark blue night sky with a full moon.

SiteName: The Crossroads of the Danforth BIA
Description: The Crossroads of the Danforth BIA was established in 2008 to serve businesses along the Danforth from Victoria Park to Scotia Avenue. The area is especially notable for its automotive businesses. Every year, the BIA presents the Wheels on the Danforth and Light up the Crossroads events.
ImageAltText: A black and white aerial photo of houses and various commercial and industrial buildings near the intersection of Danforth Avenue and Danforth Road.

Description: Painted by Magicfinnga WonG, the mural depicts a great horned owl. Below the owl are a number of circular images that include cosmos, landscapes and depictions of fish and feathers painted in the West Coast Art style.
ImageAltText: Close up of a painted mural's realistic portrait of a great horned owl with a woodland scene and a celestial galaxy enclosed in stylized circles nestled in its neck feathers.

Description: Artist De Anne Lamirande's inspiration for the mural on the wall of Chopstick Foods lies in her appreciation of the environment. She believes sharing art with the community inspires others and creates involvement. Bees and a monarch butterfly were incorporated in the design to bring awareness to saving these species. Lilies are a tribute to the owner of Chopstick Foods, Lili. A community event was also a part of this mural as area residents and children added their own brush strokes to the mural. It was created with support from the Crossroads of the Danforth BIA and StreetARToronto, and was selected as best mural by the Toronto Association of Business Improvement Areas.
ImageAltText: A vibrant painted mural stretches across an exterior wall of a building and depicts two bees and a monarch butterfly perched on many purple daisies that surround two pink lilies.

Description: Oakridge Park is a gathering spot in the community with a baseball diamond, a multipurpose sports field, splash pad and a children's playground. Annually, the local Crossroads of the Danforth BIA organizes Wheels on The Danforth and Festival in the Park, a summer festival featuring classic cars, hot rods and motorcycles, entertainment, a bicycle tour, children's area, marketplace and more.
ImageAltText: A black line illustration of a coniferous tree and a leafy tree beside a swing set.

Description: Mann Gatehouse was built to the north of Donald Mann's estate mansion. While Mann's house burned down in the 1930s, the gatehouse remains and has been converted into a private dwelling. Donald Mann was a Canadian railway contractor and entrepreneur. Partnering with William Mackenzie, he built railway lines in western Canada, the United States, Brazil and China. In 1895, Mann and Mackenzie began purchasing and building the lines in western Canada which would later become the Canadian Northern Railway (CNoR), a system that would stretch from Vancouver Island to Cape Breton Island and form Canada's second transcontinental railway system.
ImageAltText: A black and white historic photo of the exterior of the former three-storey mansion of Donald Mann, which features wooden latticework on the first floor windows and ivy climbing the walls.

Description: Scarborough Council had meetings on the second storey of this building from 1922 to the late 1940s, when Scarborough was still incorporated as a township. It was soon after that Scarborough became a part of Metropolitan Toronto and then later amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998. This building serves as a reminder that from the mid-19th century to the mid-20th century, Scarborough was a separate municipality from the City of Toronto with its own representatives and council. Today, Scarborough Community Council, comprising of Toronto City Councillors in Scarborough wards, meets at the Scarborough Civic Centre.
ImageAltText: A black and white historic street view photo of a two-storey brick building with a corner entranceway, windows with stone lintels, and a wraparound sign identifying it as The Canadian Bank of Commerce.

Description: Birchmount Fire Hall was the first fire hall in Scarborough. It was built in 1925, housing the township's first fire department and the first police department. Today it is recognized as a historic site, which houses a museum to preserve the local firefighting history. The museum collection can be viewed by appointment.
ImageAltText: Street view of the Birchmount Fire Hall Museum's red brick building with a tower on the right side, green trim windows and roof, and two red garage doors.

Description: This sports, health and fitness centre is open to all members of the community. A central focus of Variety Village is to help young people with disabilities and those who face developmental barriers through integrated sports, life skills programs and other activities. A Toronto-based Variety Club opened Variety Village over 65 years ago as a vocational and training school and residence for youth. Then in 1981, Variety Village reopened its doors as a world class indoor sports facility with adapted physical education, swim classes, track and field, basketball court, three-tiered Children in Motion activity program and more.
ImageAltText: Behind a rounded parking lot and driveway with five vehicles is the modern Variety Village building, which features a large, rounded front portico and two narrow central towers.

Description: In 1927, a group of entertainers began the Variety Club in Pittsburgh, which helped other entertainers and supported civic initiatives. In 1928, the theatre manager of the Sheridan Square Theatre found an infant named Catherine abandoned in the theatre, and the Variety Club members acted as guardians to support her until she was adopted at the age of five. The group continued to help children in need, and now it is a multinational children's charity with 14,000 members in 14 countries.
ImageAltText: None

Description: Scarborough Bluffs Refreshment Room, once commonly known as Stinson's Shop, was a Scarborough landmark. In the late 19th century, Cliffside, the area between Kingston Road and Lake Ontario, became a popular recreational destination. In response, commercial buildings were developed and transit lines were improved in the area. Scarborough Bluffs Refreshment Room was opened by Albert Stinson in 1903 to attract disembarking passengers from the nearby radial car stop. The building received a heritage designation in 2008, as it is a rare surviving example of the recreational and transportation history of Scarborough and has a wood-frame structure, dormers and windows typical of the time. It now houses Stop 14, a home decor shop named after the building's former radial car stop number.
ImageAltText: Historic black and white exterior photo of a two-storey wood frame building with four people in early twentieth century clothing posing at the corner door under a sign reading "Scarboro Bluffs Refreshment Room A. Stinson".

Description: On July 1, 1893 the Toronto and Scarboro' Electric Railway, Light and Power commenced operating an electric street railway or Radial Car line from Queen Street East to Blantyre Avenue, east of Victoria Park. The line opened as part of Canada Day (then called Dominion Day) celebrations, and 12,000 tickets were sold for the first day. Although it is doubtful that all of the ticket holders rode the radial that day, Toronto's Archbishop did get a turn. In 1898, the route was relaid, and over the next decade continued to stretch eastward to West Hill, becoming the Scarboro Division of the Toronto & York Radial Railways in 1904. In 1921, the Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) replaced the line with its streetcar service to Birchmount Road. While the radial extended to West Hill, this section between Birchmount and Eglinton closed in 1936 and was never reestablished by the TTC.
ImageAltText: Black and white historical photo of a radial car filled with passengers parked on a radial track, with a ticket taker and passenger about to disembark.

Description: This was the home of two Canadian artists, Frederick and Louise Coates. Frederick Coates was born in 1890 and moved to Canada in 1913. He worked as a model-maker, sculptor and an art director at Hart House Theatre. His large linocut mural can still be seen in the theatre lobby. Louise Coates was born in 1889 and she was Frederick's lifelong collaborator. The couple built and lived in this medieval cottage-style house overlooking the Scarborough Bluffs. They were known to host masquerades and theatrical and musical performances in their house. When Frederick Coates first purchased the lot, Chine Drive was largely undeveloped. There is a wooded ravine running to the west, which the southern portion of the street follows to its end.
ImageAltText: A black line illustration of a two-storey historic house with a dark roof and slender chimney.

Description: In 1890, the idea was conceived to build a seminary, which would provide English-speaking priests to parishes throughout Canada. After various fundraising campaigns, construction of St. Augustine's Seminary began in 1910. Completed three years later and able to accommodate 100 students, the seminary was dedicated on August 28, 1913. St. Augustine's became not only the first seminary in English-speaking Canada but also the first institution of higher education in Scarborough. The building is in the Beaux Arts style with influences from the Renaissance Classical tradition.
ImageAltText: Aerial photo of a sprawling Beaux Arts-style historical semenary with a large central octagonal steeple, as well as the surrounding grounds, trees and a winding path.

SiteName: Heritage Minute: Motels of Kingston Road
Description: This utility box mural, painted by artist Kyla Ross as part of StreetARToronto's Outside the Box Program, depicts the signs of the area's many well-known motels, some of which still remain today. Kingston Road's centuries-old history as a travel route resulted in many inns and taverns being built along the road. By the 1950s, motels replaced many of the old inns because of the prevalence of the car and the trend in road-tripping. Also due to its proximity to the Scarborough Bluffs, the motel business on Kingston Road was booming. But by the 1980s, with new major highways established nearby, the motels lost business. Many of the motel buildings were then co-opted by the City for use as overflow housing from the City's shelter system and as transitional housing for newcomers to Canada.
Address: Kingston Rd. and Brimley Rd. S.
ImageAltText: A utility box covered by a painted mural featuring a black background and a variety of colourful historic signs for motels that used to be on Kingston Road.

Description: Scarborough Village Theatre is home to Theatre Scarborough, which consists of three theatre companies: Scarborough Players, Scarborough Music Theatre and Scarborough Theatre Guild. Theatre Scarborough has managed the shared theatre space for over 35 years, however the history of the companies dates back even further. Scarborough Theatre Guild was formed in 1959 and ten years later moved into an old church on Denton Avenue. They were soon joined by Scarborough Players, who also formed in 1959. Scarborough Music Theatre evolved out of the Church of the Master Senior Choir's concerts in the early 1960s.
ImageAltText: Black line illustration of a wide one-storey building with three distinct sections and an entrance overhang with a sign that reads "Village Theatre".

SiteName: Universal Declaration of Human Rights Article #27 Mural
Description: Created in summer 2008 by local youth, this mural symbolizes the evolution of community as it celebrates strength and diversity through creative participation. The mural includes a map of the world and people engaged in a number of arts and creative activities. It is part of Amnesty International's Project Urban Canvas and pays homage to Article #27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: 'Everyone has the right freely to participate in the cultural life of the community, to enjoy the arts and to share in scientific advancement and its benefits.'
ImageAltText: A colourful painted mural extending around an exterior corner of a brick building, depicting the Scarborough Bluffs and shoreline with a map of the world along the skyline, and beneath that a scene of people engaging in arts activities.

Description: The Cornell and Campbell families had a significant impact on the development of Scarborough. William Cornell, a descendant of a Rhode Island colonist who came to America in 1736, settled here on two lakefront-lots in the forest in 1799. With other pioneers he cut out a road, which later became Kingston Road, planted the first orchard and built the first grist (grain) and saw mill in the township. His descendants continued to make notable contributions to the development of Scarborough. Edward Cornell was a member of the township's first municipal council in 1850. James G. Cornell served as Reeve (1913-1919), Warden of York County, and trustee of Scarborough's first high school (1920-1932). In 1944, the old farm house became the home of Helen Campbell, a Cornell descendant, and her husband Albert M. Campbell, who served as Reeve of Scarborough (1957-1966), Mayor (1967-1969) and chairman of the Metro Toronto Council (1970-1973).
ImageAltText: Behind a long front lawn with two colourful flowered garden beds with white vegetative trim, the two-storey red brick Cornell Campbell House is partially obscured by leafy trees.

Description: Washington Manse is also called Washington Parsonage or Chester House. It was built in 1875 and enlarged in 1893. This was the first parsonage built by the Washington Methodist congregation in Scarborough. The building is a 19th century Gothic Vernacular structure.
ImageAltText: Behind a snow-covered front lawn, the two-storey Washington Manse features decorative brickwork and detailed white trim on the central gable and front veranda.

SiteName: Boys & Girls Club East Scarborough Pillars
Description: You can see a series of murals painted onto the pillars of the fence that stretches across this large property on Kingston Road. The mural is part of Amnesty International's Project Urban Canvas and depicts Article 24: 'Everyone has the right to rest and leisure.' It depicts images of people reading, gardening, and relaxing on a beach. The project was a partnership between POR AMOR and the Boys and Girls Club of East Scarborough.
ImageAltText: A stone pillar connecting a black metal fence features a painted mural of a stylized tree with curling branches and green leaves against a red and yellow background.

Description: Offering a spectacular view of Lake Ontario from the top of the bluffs, Rosetta McClain Gardens features rose gardens and a rock fountain surrounded by a large pergola with vines. There are many benches throughout the park to sit on and enjoy the surroundings. There are over 100 species of birds that have been spotted in the park. It is the only park in Toronto that has plaques on the trees to identify their name and species. Walk to the west side of the park to find the plaques.
ImageAltText: A rock sculpture fountain in Rosetta McClain Gardens is surrounded by colourful flowers and vegetation and bordered by a paved path, large planters with flowers, and a rounded pergola.

Description: Bluffer's Park is a south Scarborough gem. There are activities for the whole family, including fishing from the shore, hiking, birdwatching, picnicking and more. The bluffs stretch for about 14 kilometres along the Lake Ontario shore. Follow the trails to enjoy both the beach and the bluffs' geological treasures. When you reach the end of the trail, look up to the west to find the most photographed point of Bluffer's Park and enjoy the magnificent and jutting edges of the bluffs. The Scarborough Bluffs are made up of 11 distinct parks, some of which offer a spectacular view of Lake Ontario, the marina and the beach. Popular photo spots include the lookout point at Cathedral Bluffs Park and Scarborough Bluffs Park. Cathedral Bluffs Park is the highest point of the bluffs standing 90-metres above the shore. This lookout is accessible when walking east from the south end of Broadmead Avenue. To access the Scarborough Bluffs Park lookout, walk south from the south end of Scarboro Crescent.
ImageAltText: Distant view of a portion of the Scarborough Bluffs partially covered by vegetation against the shoreline of Lake Ontario.

Description: The trail follows nearly 24 hectares of ravine and descends about 90 metres in elevation from the top of the Scarborough Bluffs down toward Lake Ontario. While some sections of Bellamy Creek have been channelized in engineering projects, much of the creek is also a natural stream. The area is largely populated by native tree species like white and yellow birch, American beech, white oak and sugar maple, and is home to a diversity of wildlife including white-tailed deer, beavers, foxes and coyotes. There are also over 100 species of birds that have been spotted on the trail.
ImageAltText: In front of a muddy patch of ground and a forested area with bare trees, a painted wooden sign on two posts reads "Doris McCarthy Trail" in yellow lettering.

Description: Gates Gully, now known as Bellamy Ravine, is part of the Doris McCarthy Trail extending from Kingston Road to Lake Ontario. During the 1830s, it was known as a harbour for smugglers from the United States avoiding import taxes on tea, tobacco and contraband. The trail was located behind Gates Inn and Tavern, built by early settler Jonathan Gates in 1820. The inn was a favourite of the Scarborough militia that fought William Lyon Mackenzie's rebels in the Upper Canada Rebellion.
ImageAltText: None

Description: Doris Jean McCarthy was born in 1910 in Calgary, Alberta and spent more than 70 years living in her home atop the Scarborough Bluffs, affectionately named Fool's Paradise. In 1939, McCarthy bought 12 acres overlooking the Bluffs. McCarthy's mother called the property a 'fool's paradise' because she thought the purchase was an excessive spend for the then young art teacher. But after Doris McCarthy designed and built the home, completed in 1946, it became a symbol of her creativity. Fool's Paradise nurtured McCarthy's artistic process and she wanted to give other artists an opportunity to live and work at the site that fostered so much of her own artistic expression. To that end, she bequeathed Fool's Paradise to the Ontario Heritage Trust, which established the Doris McCarthy Artist-in-Residence Centre. This unique, living and working incubator for visual artists of all disciplines offers privacy and an opportunity for creative concentration. Fool's Paradise is occasionally open to the public for events such as Doors Open Toronto. McCarthy graduated from the University of Toronto Scarborough in 1989. Although she travelled to and painted in five continents, she is best known and celebrated for her Canadian landscapes. She was a beloved artist, writer and teacher and through her body of work and the legacy of Fool's Paradise, she continues to inspire a generation of Canadian artists.
ImageAltText: Exterior corner view of a one-storey L-shaped house with a rounded side wall in the foreground, a tall chimney at the centre and a raised flagstone front patio.

Description: Passage, by Marlene Hilton Moore, celebrates Doris McCarthy. Passage is a steel sculpture inspired by the rib cage of a fish and the ribs of a canoe. The sculpture is part of a series celebrating people and places linked together by the theme of passage: a fish's passage through water, and a canoe's passage through our environment. The interior base depicts an architectural scale ruler, with a stylized end resembling Ontario's provincial flower, the trillium.
ImageAltText: With bluffs and shoreline visible in the backround, a large steel art piece in a grassy area is mounted on two base beams with the beams above it curved into a long, horizontal ribcage shape.

Description: The Scarborough Bluffs are a geological treasure and one of the most iconic sites in Scarborough. Layers of sand and clay expose a geological record of the last stages of the Great Ice Age. Many fossils of plants and animals have been discovered in the sediment on the first 46 metres, which formed around 70,000 years ago. On top of this sediment, 61 metres of alternating layers of clay and sand reveal the alternating timeline of glaciers advancing and retreating until about 12,000 years ago. The parks that make up the Scarborough Bluffs stretch from Rosetta McClain Gardens to East Point Park and contain meadow, forest, beach and wetland habitats. The parks are home to a number of unique plant and wildlife species. The Scarborough Bluffs are a crucial stopover site for migrating birds, providing food and shelter to birds that are resting before and after their seasonal migration over Lake Ontario. While enjoying the trails along Scarborough's lakefront, keep an eye and an ear out for birds and other wildlife.
ImageAltText: Aerial view from Lake Ontario of the Scarborough Bluffs, surrounding trees and vegetation, and the Bluffer's Park grounds along the lower shoreline.

Description: After the Second World War, Rosa and Spencer Clark sold over 400 acres to be developed as the Guildwood Village subdivision, which officially opened in 1957. The Clarks had a clear vision for the subdivision, which included environmentally responsive residential developments, making Guildwood unique in Toronto. For example, homes were planned around existing, mature trees and wires were placed underground to keep the look of the community as natural as possible. The grand gates to the subdivision on Kingston Road were originally forged in England in 1839 for Toronto's Stanley Barracks, which was located west of Fort York where the Canadian National Exhibition is now. The barracks were demolished in 1953 and the gates relocated to Scarborough as the grand entrance to Guildwood Village.
ImageAltText: Street view of three narrow stone pillars with black metal fencing connecting them, and a banner hanging above the central pillar that reads "The Guild Gardens and Waterfront Park".

Description: This scenic and historic 36-hectare park, formerly Guildwood Park, is a sculpture sanctuary within beautiful gardens. It has an interesting history that reflects famous artists, powerful political figures and contributions made to the art community. The land was transformed into gardens and parkland by Rosa and Spencer Clark in the 1930s. The property and the architectural fragments ornamenting the gardens were sold to the Metro Toronto and Region Conservation Authority and the Province of Ontario in 1978 to be maintained as a public park. The land is also significant for its rare tract of Carolinian forest. Today there are efforts by the City of Toronto and community organizations to protect this forested area and the animals that it supports. The park is an important site for migratory and nesting birds, and mammals such as deer and fox.
ImageAltText: A historic architectural stone fragment with several ornate bronze figures in a shady, grassy area behind two colourful flower planters and a row of black-eyed Susan flowers.

Description: The Sculptor's Cabin was built in 1940 by Danish wood sculptor Aage Madsen. It is the last remaining example of one of the many cabins built to house artists for the Guild of All Arts. Over the years, it has been home and studio for many sculpture artists. Local Scarborough artist Dorsey James carved the Norse mythology ornamentation on the face of the building in 1979.
ImageAltText: Front exterior of a small wood cabin with several ornamental wood carvings shaped as Norse mythological figures and a window protected by thin metal bars.

Description: There are many architecture fragments that trace the history of Toronto. Look for the Temple Building fragment. When the original building first opened in downtown Toronto, it was one of Toronto's first skyscrapers and was the highest building in the British Empire. It housed the office of the Independent Order of Foresters (IOF) at the time that Dr. Oronhyatekha (1841-1907), a Mohawk physician and scholar, was the Chief Ranger of the organization. The building was demolished in 1970, but you can still see this history reflected in the ornate IOF initials that are carved in the red sandstone blocks under the moose's head.
ImageAltText: On a concrete base in a grassy area, a sandstone fragment of a building with the words "Temple Building" engraved along the bottom and decorative relief patterns engraved into the three pillars above it.

Description: The Guild Inn Estate (Bickford House) General Harold Child Bickford purchased the property in 1914, named it Ranelagh Park Country Estate and built the well-known Bickford House. Today, the Bickford House is a designated heritage property, and considered an excellent example of early 20th century Period Revival style with Arts and Crafts detailing. In 1932, Rosa and Spencer Clark founded the Guild of All Arts after Rosa purchased 450 acres of land. The Guild of All Arts, mainly located in the Bickford House, was an artist colony that contained a shop, a tea room, and studios in fine art and craft, including painting, sculpture, hand loom weaving, tooled leather, ceramics, metal work, wood carving and batik. After the war, the Clarks expanded the colony to include a hotel, restaurant and formal gardens. The area became known as the Guild Inn or the Guild. During Toronto's building boom that began in the 1960s, many historic 19th and 20th century downtown buildings were demolished. As an advocate for architectural preservation, Spencer Clark recovered many of these buildings' facades and architectural features and displayed them on the grounds of the Guild. The park and monuments were sold to the Metro Toronto and Region Conservation Authority in 1978. The hotel continued to be run by Spencer Clark until 1983. In 2017, Bickford House was restored and reopened as The Guild Inn Estate, featuring newly built east and west wings, a restaurant, a banquet hall and ample event space.
ImageAltText: Front exterior view of the restored Bickford House of The Guild Inn Estate featuring painted white walls and a large central portico made of wood and stone.

Description: During the Second World War, the Canadian government leased the Guild Inn and surrounding property and turned it into a training base for the Women's Royal Naval Service (WRENS). The hotel served as a military hospital for victims of post-traumatic stress disorder. The arts and craft facilities provided therapeutic rehabilitation for the service personnel undergoing treatment there.
Address: The Guild Inn Estate, 201 Guildwood Pkwy.
ImageAltText: None

Description: The Clark Centre for the Arts, opening in 2022, is a City-run creative centre that features arts studios and programming, a hallway gallery and multipurpose space in a large-scale addition to and rehabilitation of the existing structure. Formerly known as Building 191, it was originally designed and built in 1963 for use as administrative offices and storage for the Guild of All Arts. While the original two-storey concrete block and steel structure is very plain, it is ornamented by two large bas-relief panels from the historic 1938 Globe and Mail building and the Marguetta stone originally from the University Avenue Armouries built in 1891.
ImageAltText: Behind a garden with several decorative architectural fragments, the modern third-storey addition to the Clark Centre for the Arts partially overhangs the renovated structure, with two large bas-relief panels and historic stonework ornamenting the front side.

Description: The Clarks built an open-air theatre from remnants of the historic Bank of Toronto building, which was demolished around 1960. The stage is adorned with eight limestone columns, and Corinthian capitals and arches that were repurposed from the facade of the building. Today, the Greek Theatre is used for events all year round and animated by the Guild Festival Theatre in the summer.
ImageAltText: Surrounded by grass, bushes and trees, a historic limestone building fragment shaped like a rounded stage, with eight columns and Corinthian-style detailing and arches.

Description: The log cabin was built in approximately 1850. It is commonly referred to as the Osterhout Cabin. The site was provisioned to William Osterhout in 1805, but the property exchanged hands many times before the cabin was even built. It was later purchased with the property by Rosa and Spencer Clark, and modernized to be used as an artist residence and studio at the Guild of All Arts. It was last occupied by sculptor Elizabeth Fraser Williamson, who used the cabin as a studio into the 1990s. Today, the cabin is part of the Clark Centre for the Arts, operated by the City of Toronto, Arts Services.
ImageAltText: A log cabin with a white framed window and painted white door is partially obscured by bushes, and a stone pillar with an inset plaque is visible in the foreground.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description:
Black Urbanism Toronto (BUTO) is a non-profit organization founded in 2018, which works to advance the economic, social and cultural interests of Black communities in Toronto. BUTO supports and engages Black residents and business owners in Little Jamaica to participate in community development, and they co-authored a report with the Studio of Contemporary Architecture and Open Architecture Collaborative Canada called 'A Black Business Conversation: On Planning for the Future of Black Business and Residents on Eglinton Ave. West'. This report has informed and is intended to guide future community planning and economic development of the neighbourhood. 

BUTO also assists businesses with several initiatives. The Pathways to Community Ownership initiative is looking to increase property ownership within the Black community by means of a Black-led Community Land Trust model, which will improve the capacity of local business owners and maintain the area's cultural and economic core. Through the Black Business Grant, launched during the COVID-19 pandemic in partnership with other local partners, BUTO raised funds for Black-owned businesses along Eglinton West to support economic recovery from the pandemic and setbacks from the years of the Eglinton Crosstown LRT construction.
ImageAltText: A white door with a round sign of the Black Urbanism Toronto logo on a grey tile building.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Opened in 1978, the station is particularly notable for its distinctive architectural features. The ceiling is a large concrete slab with skylights set into the waffle-like design. The large glass windows around the entrance are designed to make the ceiling appear to float. The station has sand-blasted concrete and brick wall finishes instead of the usual subway tile, and it has windows at platform level to let in natural light. In 2009, a green roof was installed on the platforms to make the building more environmentally friendly and to combat challenges with rainwater run-off. When the Eglinton Crosstown LRT opens, the station will be renamed Cedarvale Station. The station's artwork can be seen at platform level, with a pair of two-storey enamel murals called Summertime Streetcar by Gerald Zeldin, which depict 1930s streetcars from various angles. A public art piece by Douglas Coupland, called Super Signals, will also be installed in Cedarvale Station, and will feature aluminum panels with colourful concentric circles on black and white diagonal lines that resemble the TTC's wayfinding graphics.
ImageAltText: Photo of a two storey art installation at platform level

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Throughout the summer months, the Afro-Caribbean Farmers' Market enlivens Reggae Lane and supports Black business owners with vendors selling prepared foods, baked goods, preserves, lifestyle items, produce from the Caribbean islands and African countries and seasonal produce grown locally. The market began in 2017 near Jane Street and Wilson Avenue, and then launched in Little Jamaica in 2021. The Afro-Caribbean Farmers' Market works with local partners and artists to animate the weekly market and to showcase performers and musicians from the neighbourhood. The Market is a focal point of the community and plays a key role for residents and visitors to celebrate and connect with Afro-Caribbean diasporic cultures.
ImageAltText: A snapshot of the AfroCarribean Farmer's Market with a white vendor tent surrounded by shoppers.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description:
Reggae Lane was designated in 2015 to celebrate the musical legacy of Little Jamaica. An impressive 1,200-square-foot mural was collaboratively designed by artist Adrian Hayles, who mentored local youth, in consultation with prominent reggae musicians and reggae music experts. It was produced in partnership with STEPS Public Art and The Laneway Project.  

The design is a celebration of Toronto's reggae traditions, depicting Little Jamaica resident artists, significant international reggae musicians who performed or recorded in the area, and figures and symbols in Rastafarian culture. It honours the importance of reggae music and reggae artists in creating a place for Black and Caribbean communities in Toronto, and also reflects the achievements of the Little Jamaica community and its impact on reggae and the Canadian music industry.

From left to right, the mural depicts Bob Marley, Haile Selassi, Pluggy Satchmo, Bernie Pitters, Leroy Sibbles, Lord Tanamo, Leroy Brown, Carol Brown, Otis Gayle, Joe Isaacs, Jay Douglas, Stranger Cole, Johnny Osbourn, the Lion of Juda, Jojo Bennett, Nana Mclean and Jackie Mittoo. Many of the musicians depicted in the mural recorded and performed, or established music studios and record shops, in Little Jamaica. Also referenced is Toronto-based CFRB radio station, which was the first mainstream station in Canada to play reggae music on a specialty program in the 1970s. At this time, it was one of the country's most popular radio stations.
ImageAltText: A segment of the colourful painted Reggae Lane mural featuring reggae icons Bernie Pitters, Leroy Sibbles and Lord Tanamo.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: TreaJah Isle is a record store and juice bar that has operated in Little Jamaica for over 25 years. Its founder, Nana McLean, is a legendary reggae artist, and is considered Canada's Queen of Reggae. Nana McLean received a JUNO Award in 1997 for Best Reggae Recording, was inducted to the Reggae Hall of Fame in 2016, and continues to release new albums and singles. In honour of her music career and significance to the Little Jamaica community, her portrait is featured in the Reggae Lane mural across the street. The store was named after Treasure Isle Records, a prominent record label that was founded by Duke Reid in Jamaica. Co-owners Natty B. and Jah Chozen bought the business from Nana McLean in 1997. More recently, the store is co-owned by Shane Kenney, who is a Rastafarian and passionate about the role that TreaJah Isle plays in keeping the Rastafari and Jamaican culture alive on Eglinton West. TreaJah Isle continues to be a local hub for music fans and musicians who want to be immersed in Jamaican music culture. TreaJah Isle aims to bring music from Jamaica and the Caribbean to Toronto and to keep Jamaican culture rooted in the daily life of the community.
ImageAltText: The storefront of Trea-Jah-Isle Records and its store sign featuring an illustration of the Lion of Judah against a backdrop of three painted lines of green, yellow and red.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: In the 1980s, before opening RAPS restaurant, Horace 'Rap' Rose was a music producer working with notable reggae artists such as Dennis Brown and Gregory Isaacs. He also ran Joe Gibbs Records on Eglinton Avenue West. While on tour with musician Johnny Osborne, Horace noticed that after late-night performances, musicians and industry professionals often required meals, but restaurants were closed for the day. After identifying this need within the music community, he opened RAPS in 1982, which became known for its long open hours that stretch into the early morning to serve musicians and those out late attending performances. RAPS prepares traditional Jamaican cuisine, and the jerk chicken is smoked outside in a steel oil drum, which invites passersby into the restaurant for a bite.
ImageAltText: The storefront of Rap's Chicken. Jerk chicken is smoked outside in a steel oil drum.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: The Grammy Award-Winning Jamaican reggae group Black Uhuru released a song called 'Youth of Eglington' on their album Red in 1981. At this time, Michael Rose, brother to Horace Rose, who founded the local restaurant RAPS, was a lead vocalist for Black Uhuru. The song references gun crime on Eglinton West and was an appeal for youth to reject violence. It was also created in response to gun violence in Brooklyn (United States), Brixton (England) and Kingston (Jamaica) at that time.
ImageAltText: An illustration by Doug Rodas of Jamaican reggae group Black Uhuru members, Derek "Duckie" Simpson, Sandra "Puma" Jones, and Michael Rose.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: The More Than a Haircut program was established in 2006, as a partnership between the Macaulay Child Development Centre and community leaders, to foster social connection and information sharing for Black fathers by holding a series of conversations in barbershops along Eglinton Avenue West and around the city. The program operates from several barbershops along Eglinton West. Barbershops are an important cultural space within the Black community and as essential meeting places for Black men and fathers to socialize, exchange ideas and participate in the community.
ImageAltText: The storefront of More than a Hair Cut and its store sign featuring an illustration of many people getting a haircut and a slogan that says "Where we cater to all your needs"

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Monica's Beauty Supply played a key role in the development and life of the community in Little Jamaica. First operating as a record store before becoming a beauty supply shop in the 1980s, Monica's has been central to the establishment of the music industry in Little Jamaica, influencing both reggae and hip-hop music culture. For decades, Monica and George Lewis operated a record store, George the Record Man, known for its large record collection that made it a destination for musicians and music lovers across the city. They not only sold the latest records from Jamaica, but also had some of the first hip-hop records from pioneering artists available in Canada. The records inspired and influenced the sound of celebrated local artists, such as  hip-hop artist Michie Mee, and helped develop the industry in Canada. George and Monica also started a recording studio and production company, Monica's Productions (later Scorpio Records) that produced music with local artists and musicians from abroad, providing opportunities for Black artists that were often excluded at major studios and record labels. Monica's Beauty Salon & Cosmetic Supply was a foundational community hub for decades, providing products and services for Black and Caribbean communities in Toronto.
ImageAltText: An illustration by Doug Rodas of Monica's Beauty Supply featuring a woman holding onto a haircomb next to a shelf of various beauty products.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Randy Fung, Raymond Fung and Donald Lee-Sue, who were Jamaican immigrants to Canada, founded Randy's Take-Out at this location, which became one of the best-known Jamaican eateries in Toronto, and a destination for residents and visitors to the city. Opening in 1979, Randy's Take-Out has been a staple of the neighbourhood, operating for over 40 years. Randy's Take-Out closed its doors in early 2022 due to aging owners, as well as impacts from the Eglinton Crosstown LRT construction and the pandemic, but it reopened in the same location in 2024.   Randy's continues to be an anchor business in the Little Jamaica community. It was one of the first businesses to introduce Jamaican patties to Toronto, which have since become one of the city's staple dishes.
ImageAltText: An Illustration by Doug Rodas of a woman with a box of patties and a can of soda, holding onto a patty with her right hand up close to her mouth at Randy's Takeout

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Vernal Small, owner of Jamall Caribbean Custom Tailors, has been a tailor for over 50 years and he is renowned in Little Jamaica for his custom suits and tuxedos. The business has been located at Eglinton Avenue West and Oakwood Avenue for over four decades, and serves both regular and new customers each day. Like many of the integral businesses in the Little Jamaica community, Jamall Caribbean Custom Tailors was operating during the height of Little Jamaica's music scene, when the area was a hub for musicians to record tracks, rehearse and perform.
ImageAltText: The Storefront of Jamall Carribean Custom Tailor featuring a buliding with  large mint green tiles, a large vertical rectangular window with the door on the right with an open sign. Above the window is the store's sign with the following red text: JAMALL Carribean Custom Tailor, 611 & 609 OAKWOOD AVE, 416-781-1685. Brown bricks surround the upper levels of the building.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Along the laneway is the Welcome to Reggae Lane mural, which was painted in 2016 by artist Adrian Hayles. The mural marks and celebrates the renamed Reggae Lane, with the street name written in a cursive font across the mural. It depicts a woman listening to music and includes references to the neighbourhood's connection to Jamaica and the music industry, such as the stacked speakers, which were innovative custom-built sound systems developed in Jamaica by local DJs, MCs, musicians and sound engineers for dance parties and competitions, and greatly influenced the development of ska, dancehall, reggae and dub.
ImageAltText: A colourful painted mural on the side of a building wall with black cursive text outlined in yellow reading "Welcome to Reggae Lane" at the top left side of the mural and a woman listening to music with headphones on. There are houses and a subway train in the background and a family with children on the bottom left side.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Accordions Canada was founded by Matt De Florio, a professional accordionist, teacher and an author of numerous method books. Throughout the 1950s, Matt was featured weekly on the CBC television network. He opened his own business in 1958 called De Florio Imports, which sold accordions and other instruments that were imported from Italy. The name was  changed to Musical Instruments of Canada in the 1960s. During this time, Matt's son Rudy worked at the store and was tasked with instrument repairs. Rudy now operates the business with his own sons, Chris and Shawn. Over the years, Musical Instruments of Canada became known as an accordion destination and the decision was made to specialize only in that instrument. This resulted in adopting the Accordions Canada name to better represent its identity. For over 60 years, Accordions Canada has been selling and servicing accordions on Eglinton West.
ImageAltText: The storefront of Accordions Canada founded by Matt De Florio, specializing in Accordions, nested on the second floor of the building with the store Latina Dress below it.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Nathan and Goldie Redmon were the first Black entrepreneurs in York to establish their own carriage business, Redmon Haulage, which was located on Belgravia Avenue in a home designed and built by Nathan Redmon. Nathan Redmon came to Toronto from the United States in 1913 and worked as a sleeping car porter. After saving his money for several years, Redmon started the haulage business in 1918, which grew to the second largest trucking and carriage business in York Township by 1937. Redmon Haulage operated for 36 years.
Address: Eglinton Ave. W. and Times Rd.
ImageCredit: Alfred Pearson, City of Toronto Archives, 1924
ImageAltText: A vintage photograph of York Eglinton Ave looking West from Dufferin & Vaughn taken on Oct 17, 1924 with shops on the left side with 2 vintage automobiles parked on the side of the road.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description:
The Black Business and Professional Association (BBPA) supports educational and professional growth, recognizes excellence and provides opportunities for Black entrepreneurs and professionals in Black communities across Canada. It was founded in 1982 by Denham Jolly, who brought together members of the Black community in Toronto to form the association. 

In 2021, the BBPA opened this new storefront location in Little Jamaica. The Government of Canada announced a $1 million investment over three years for the revitalization of Little Jamaica through its FedDev Ontario program. This investment was provided to the BBPA by the City of Toronto to deliver programs and initiatives to support Black-owned and operated businesses within Little Jamaica. The organization works with local community partners and BIAs to deliver these programs and initiatives, such as Sinting Fest on Eglinton West, a multi-day festival started in 2022 to revitalize Eglinton West by highlighting businesses, entrepreneurs, culture, local organizations and artists.
ImageAltText: The storefront of Black Business and Professional Association (BBPA) in a two-storey black painted brick building with a black and white sign

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Studio M, operated by Masani Productions, is a photography and recording studio that hosts arts and cultural events, such as the Canadian Reggae Music Conference, the Rastafest Reggae Music Festival and Sistahfest, which is a festival celebrating International Women's Day that showcases artists and industry professionals through performances and professional conferences. The studio can also be booked for music and video productions, as well as offering space for community-based events, dance and music classes. Since 1980, Masani Productions has been producing, promoting and distributing books, films, videos and records in Jamaica and Canada, and also focuses on artist development and small business management.
ImageAltText: The storefront of Studio M with a colourful sign on a two floor brown brick building.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Commissioned by the York-Eglinton BIA, this mural was designed and painted by Ryan Smeeton to celebrate the cultural diversity of the area. The mural depicts a hand reaching toward a large Rose of Sharon, a type of hibiscus flower and a biblical symbol referenced in some reggae music. The purple flowers that appear in the mural are Lignum Vitae, the national flower of Jamaica. The use of natural imagery in the mural also speaks to the natural features of the area, including the Cedarvale Ravine and the Beltline Trail.
ImageAltText: A large exterior wall mural showcasing a hand reaching out toward pink and purple flowers against a pastel-toned backdrop.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description:
This vibrant mural on the front corner of the John Howard Society building was commissioned by the York-Eglinton BIA and designed and executed by Koe Design, the studio of artist Kayla Whitney. The design features many brightly coloured flowers associated with the heritage and cultures represented in the community, and it is intended to uplift, inspire and unify the neighbourhood. 

The John Howard Society is a non-profit organization that advocates for and supports people and communities affected by the criminal justice system. The organization delivers programs and services focused on prevention, intervention and re-integration and advocates for change in the criminal justice process.
ImageAltText: Mural on the corner of a building featuring a navy blue background and many brightly coloured flowers.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: The York-Eglinton Business Improvement Area (BIA) was formed in 1981 and has a membership of over 200 businesses along Eglinton West from Marlee Avenue to Dufferin Street and along the north-east side of Dufferin up to Whitmore Avenue. The BIA is responsible for several initiatives and partnerships that support and advocate for local businesses as well as coordinating public events and heritage walks throughout the year.
ImageAltText: Storefront of the York-Eglinton Business Improvement Area with a black and white identifying sign that features an illustration of an Eglinton Avenue West street sign.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: This mural was painted by artist Adrian Hayles to celebrate the local community. It depicts vegetation and herbs with the words 'Likkle Jamaica' in the foreground. 'Likkle' is a Patois word for 'Little.' The words are painted on a backdrop of a map, with the roads outlined in red, and the area of the Little Jamaica community highlighted in yellow. The artist was inspired by rice and peas, a traditional Jamaican dish, for the colour of the letters. The mural was created with support from the City of Toronto and Nine Miles of Smiles, a non-profit healthcare volunteer organization that provides free dental care to underserviced areas in Jamaica.
ImageAltText: A mural with "Likkle Jamaica" in the center painted on the backdrop of a map with roads outlined in red and the area of the Little Jamaica community highlighted in yellow, surrounding vegetation branch out from the text and a rice and peas dish sits in the bottom right.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
SiteName: Bell Box Mural by Lula Lumaj (2017)
Description: The artist directly references the area's reggae traditions through this image of a record being played with musical notes and records decorating a red, green and gold background. The colours are associated with the Ethiopian flag, which is an important symbol of Rastafarian culture referenced in reggae, in particular the flag from the reign of Haile Selassie, a former Ethiopian regent.
ImageAltText: A Bell utility box painted to depict a turntable playing a record, with music notes and three additional records floating beneath and to the right of it.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: This mural by artist Adrian Hayles celebrates the life and legacy of Ronald "Jimmy" Ashford Wisdom, who was a barber, musician and community leader. Wisdom's Barbershop and Hair Salon was an institution in Little Jamaica for three decades. Wisdom moved to Toronto from Jamaica in 1968, performing as a soul singer in clubs before becoming a full-time barber and opening his own business in 1980. The mural marks the renamed street 'Jimmy Wisdom Way,' which was named in Wisdom's honour after he passed away in 2019. The renaming of the street, along with the commissioning of the mural, was led by City Councillor Mike Colle's office.
ImageAltText: A mural painted by artist Adrian Hayles with "Jimmy Wisdom Way" in the center painted in gradients of Green, Orange, and Red and a background of a beach with palm trees and Jimmy Wisdom on the left and right side of the mural.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: The Centro Cultural Latinoamericano  (CCL) seeks to create opportunities for residents to engage in community and educational activities, including as a performance space for Latinx music, poetry and literature. In 2020, due to the pandemic, CCL changed their focus to addressing food insecurity in the neighbourhood, launching a food bank to support urgent community needs. The organization continues to work with community partners to deliver arts and community programs, such as workshops and events in visual arts, dance, music, as well as English classes.
ImageAltText: A two storey brown brick building of the Centro Cultural Lationamericano on the first floor hosting a Food Bank Every Friday from 2-4PM.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: The library opened as part of the Township of York Public Library Board in 1951 and was later named in honour of head librarian Maria A. Shchuka in 1997. Thanks to an extensive reconstruction in 2002, the library branch now offers many services to the community, including a youth hub, an enhanced learning centre with a full Adobe Suite and material in several languages. It is also one of four libraries across the city to house the Rita Cox Black and Caribbean Heritage Collection, one of the most significant Black and Caribbean heritage collections in Canada. It includes over 18,000 print and audiovisual materials about the Black and Caribbean historical and cultural experience.
ImageAltText: The brown brick two-storey Maria A Shchuka Library with many large windows and a front entrance with painted mint green doors.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: Dr. Rita Cox is a storyteller, author and librarian who pioneered the Toronto Public Library's Rita Cox Black and Caribbean Heritage Collection. After her retirement from the Toronto Public Library in 1995, Dr. Cox was appointed a Citizenship Court Judge by the Government of Canada. In 1997, Dr. Cox was appointed a Member of the Order of Canada for her outstanding work in storytelling and literacy.
ImageAltText: Close up of Doctor Rita Cox smiling and wearing a teal shirt with dark stripes and a green stone necklace and earrings.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
SiteName: Bell Box Mural by Brad Leitch (2017)
Description: This dynamic mural depicts a close-up rendition of a blue jay in its nest about to take flight. The blue jay is a bird native to North America, and is associated with Toronto because of the city's Major League Baseball team, the Toronto Blue Jays. The blue jay in the mural is not blue, but is painted using a red, green and gold colour palette, as a nod to the neighbourhood's reggae roots.
ImageAltText: In a parking lot, a large Bell utility box is covered by a painted mural of a blue jay taking flight in colours of black, red, green, and yellow.

LoopTourName: Little Jamaica: Art Culture and Community
Description: The Black Diamond Arts Foundation of Canada celebrates the arts and creativity of the Afro-Caribbean community in Canada and internationally, and operates The Black Diamond Art Gallery Foundation Canada, which offers a wide selection of traditional and contemporary art, artifacts and jewellery. The gallery also runs educational programs, workshops, and lectures that highlight local artists and Afrocentric arts and culture.
ImageAltText: The storefront of Black Diamond Art Gallery featuring a caged display of many traditional and contemporary art, artifacts, and jewellery.

Description:
The Tubman Centre operated in the 1970s out of a building located at 15 Robina Ave., just north of the St. Clair Avenue West and Oakwood Avenue intersection. It was one of the only cultural centres focused on serving Black diasporic communities and youth in Toronto. The Tubman Centre was named for Harriet Tubman, an American abolitionist, social activist, and a conductor on the Underground Railroad, which was a network of activists and safe houses. Tubman escaped slavery in 1849 and conducted 13 missions to help approximately 70 people escape slavery in the United States through the Underground Railroad.

The Tubman Centre was founded by Ken Jeffers, who was a member of the public service, an activist and community leader. Jeffers established the centre in an empty YMCA facility. The Tubman Centre offered many services to Black community members, including tutoring, dance, steel drum and sports programs, as well as operating as a community hub for Black residents to gather and connect. The centre had significant impact within the community and was visited by some of the greatest musicians of the era including B.B. King, Bob Marley, and Isaac Lee Hayes.
